GEO-01.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the tilt of Earth's axis, the Prime Meridian and International Date Line, how many minutes one degree of longitude equals, Bangladesh's standard time meridian (90° E), and time-difference sums.

## Earth: basic facts 🔥
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Shape | **Oblate spheroid / geoid** — flattened at the poles, bulging at the equator |
| Equatorial radius | About **6,378 km** (polar radius about 6,357 km) |
| Equatorial circumference | About **40,075 km** |
| 🔥 Rotation (আহ্নিক গতি) | **West to east**; about **23 h 56 min 4 s** (one sidereal day); causes **day and night** |
| 🔥 Revolution (বার্ষিক গতি) | About **365 days 5 h 48 min 46 s**; causes **seasons** (with the tilt) |
| 🔥 Axis tilt | **66½° to the orbital plane**, i.e. **23½° from the vertical** |
| Mean distance from the Sun | About **149.6 million km** (1 astronomical unit); sunlight takes about **8 min 20 s** |
| **Perihelion** (nearest to Sun) | Around **3 January** (about 147 million km) |
| **Aphelion** (farthest from Sun) | Around **4 July** (about 152 million km) |

- Because the year is about 365¼ days, a **leap year** of 366 days comes every 4 years (February has 29 days).

## Latitude (অক্ষাংশ) 🔥
- **Latitude** is the **angular distance north or south of the equator**. Lines of latitude are called **parallels**; they are **parallel circles**.
- Range: **0° (equator) to 90° N and 90° S (poles)**.
- 🔥 The **equator (0°)** is the **longest parallel** (a great circle); it divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
- 1° of latitude ≈ **111 km**.

| Parallel | Latitude | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Equator (বিষুবরেখা)** | **0°** | Day and night about equal all year |
| 🔥 **Tropic of Cancer (কর্কটক্রান্তি রেখা)** | **23½° N** | Sun overhead on **21 June**; **passes through the middle of Bangladesh** |
| **Tropic of Capricorn (মকরক্রান্তি রেখা)** | **23½° S** | Sun overhead on **22 December** |
| **Arctic Circle** | **66½° N** | 24-hour day in midsummer |
| **Antarctic Circle** | **66½° S** | |

## Longitude (দ্রাঘিমাংশ) 🔥
- **Longitude** is the **angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian**. Lines of longitude are **meridians**, half-circles joining the poles; all meridians are **equal in length**.
- Range: **0° to 180° E and 180° W** (360° in all).
- 🔥 **Prime Meridian (0°)** passes through the **Royal Observatory, Greenwich, London**. It was fixed at the International Meridian Conference in **1884**.
- 🔥 **International Date Line (আন্তর্জাতিক তারিখ রেখা):** roughly along **180°**, mostly through the **Pacific Ocean**; it **zig-zags** to avoid land.
  - Crossing it **from west to east** (Asia → America): **go back one day** (subtract a day).
  - Crossing it **from east to west** (America → Asia): **gain one day** (add a day).

## Longitude and time 🔥🔥
Earth turns **360° in 24 hours**, so:
- **1° of longitude = 4 minutes** of time.
- **15° of longitude = 1 hour.**
- Places **east** of Greenwich are **ahead** (time +); places **west** are **behind** (time −).
- **GMT** (Greenwich Mean Time) is now expressed as **UTC** (Coordinated Universal Time).
- **Local time** depends on the sun at each meridian; **standard time** is the time fixed for a whole country or zone.
- The world has **24 standard time zones** of 15° each (in practice, more because of half-hour zones).

**Worked examples**
1. When it is **12 noon at Greenwich**, what time is it at **90° E**? → 90 × 4 = 360 min = 6 h ahead → **6:00 pm**.
2. Time difference between **Dhaka (90° E)** and a place at **75° W**? → 90 + 75 = 165°; 165 × 4 = 660 min = **11 hours** (Dhaka ahead).
3. Two places differ in time by **2 hours**. Longitude difference? → 120 min ÷ 4 = **30°**.

## Bangladesh: location and time 🔥
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Latitude | About **20°34′ N to 26°38′ N** |
| Longitude | About **88°01′ E to 92°41′ E** |
| 🔥 **Bangladesh Standard Time (BST)** | **UTC/GMT + 6 hours**, based on the **90° E** meridian |
| Tropic of Cancer | **Crosses the middle of the country** |
| Daylight saving time | Tried once in **2009** (clocks put forward one hour from 19 June to 31 December 2009) |

- **India:** UTC + 5:30; **Nepal:** UTC + 5:45; **Myanmar:** UTC + 6:30. So Bangladesh is **30 minutes ahead of India**.
- **China** uses **one** time zone (UTC + 8) despite its size. **France** has the **most time zones** when overseas territories are counted (12); **Russia** has **11**.

## Solstices and equinoxes 🔥
| Date | Event | Sun overhead at |
|---|---|---|
| **21 March** | **Vernal (spring) equinox** — day = night everywhere | Equator |
| 🔥 **21 June** | **Summer solstice** — **longest day** in the Northern Hemisphere | **Tropic of Cancer** |
| **23 September** | **Autumnal equinox** — day = night | Equator |
| 🔥 **22 December** | **Winter solstice** — **shortest day** in the Northern Hemisphere | **Tropic of Capricorn** |

## Quick revision
- Axis tilt: **23½°** (66½° to the orbital plane).
- 1° longitude = **4 minutes**; 15° = **1 hour**.
- Prime Meridian: **Greenwich**; Date Line: about **180°**, in the Pacific.
- BST = **GMT + 6**, meridian **90° E**.
- Tropic of Cancer **23½° N** crosses Bangladesh.
- Longest day in the north: **21 June**; shortest: **22 December**.
- Equinoxes: **21 March** and **23 September**.
- Perihelion ≈ **3 January**; aphelion ≈ **4 July**.

GEO-02.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the composition and layers of the atmosphere (where the ozone layer and ionosphere are), the planetary wind belts, famous local winds (Loo, Chinook, Harmattan), and Bangladesh's climate and seasons.

## Composition of air 🔥
| Gas | Share by volume (dry air) |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Nitrogen (N₂)** | **About 78%** |
| 🔥 **Oxygen (O₂)** | **About 21%** |
| **Argon (Ar)** | About 0.93% (most common **inert/noble gas** in air) |
| **Carbon dioxide (CO₂)** | About **0.04%** (roughly 420 ppm, and rising) |
| Others | Neon, helium, methane, ozone, water vapour (varies, 0–4%), dust |

## Layers of the atmosphere (bottom → top) 🔥🔥
| Layer | Height (approx.) | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Troposphere (ট্রপোমণ্ডল)** | 0 to **about 8 km at the poles, 16–18 km at the equator** | **All weather** (clouds, rain, storms) happens here; contains most air and water vapour; **temperature falls about 6.5 °C per km** (normal lapse rate). Upper boundary: **tropopause** |
| 🔥 **Stratosphere (স্ট্র্যাটোমণ্ডল)** | Up to **about 50 km** | Contains the **ozone layer** (about **15–35 km**), which absorbs **ultraviolet (UV)** rays; temperature **rises** with height; calm air, so **jet aircraft** fly in its lower part |
| **Mesosphere** | About 50–80/85 km | **Coldest layer** (down to about −90 °C); **meteors burn up** here |
| 🔥 **Thermosphere** | About 80 to 600+ km | Temperature rises sharply; contains the **ionosphere**, which **reflects radio waves** back to Earth; **auroras** occur here; the International Space Station orbits here |
| **Exosphere** | Above about 600 km | Outermost; very thin air (hydrogen, helium) merging into space |

- Memory hook: **T-S-M-T-E** — "**T**he **S**trong **M**an **T**hrew **E**ggs".
- The ionosphere is not a separate layer; it is an electrically charged zone mostly within the thermosphere.

## Air pressure and pressure belts
- Average sea-level pressure: **1013.25 millibars (hPa)** = 76 cm of mercury. Measured with a **barometer** (invented by **Torricelli**).
- Pressure **falls with height**.
- **Isobar:** a line joining places of **equal pressure**.

| Pressure belt | Latitude | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Equatorial low** | 0°–5° N/S | **Doldrums** — calm, rising hot air |
| **Subtropical high** | About **30° N/S** | **Horse latitudes** — calm, dry; most hot deserts lie here |
| **Subpolar low** | About **60° N/S** | |
| **Polar high** | 90° N/S | Cold, sinking air |

## Winds 🔥
Wind blows from **high pressure to low pressure**. Because of Earth's rotation, the **Coriolis force** deflects winds **to the right in the Northern Hemisphere** and **to the left in the Southern Hemisphere** (**Ferrel's law**).

### Planetary (permanent) winds
| Wind | From → to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Trade winds (আয়ন বায়ু)** | Subtropical high → **equatorial low** | **North-east trades** (N. Hemisphere), **south-east trades** (S. Hemisphere); steady; helped sailing ships |
| 🔥 **Westerlies (পশ্চিমা বায়ু)** | Subtropical high → subpolar low (30°–60°) | Very strong in the Southern Hemisphere: **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Shrieking (Screaming) Sixties** |
| **Polar easterlies** | Polar high → subpolar low | Cold, dry |

### Periodic winds
- 🔥 **Monsoon (মৌসুমি বায়ু):** seasonal reversal of winds. The word comes from Arabic **"mausim" (season)**. **South-west monsoon** (summer) brings rain to South Asia and Bangladesh; **north-east monsoon** (winter) is dry.
- **Sea breeze:** from sea to land by **day**. **Land breeze:** from land to sea at **night**.

### Local winds 🔥
| Wind | Region | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Loo** | **North India, Pakistan** plains | Hot, dry summer wind |
| **Chinook** | East slopes of the **Rocky Mountains** (USA/Canada) | Warm, dry; called **"snow eater"** |
| **Foehn** | **Alps** (Switzerland) | Warm, dry |
| **Sirocco** | From the **Sahara** to Italy/Mediterranean | Hot, dusty |
| **Harmattan** | **West Africa** | Dry, dusty; called **"the doctor"** because it relieves humid heat |
| **Mistral** | Rhône valley, **France** | **Cold**, dry |
| **Khamsin** | **Egypt** | Hot, dusty |
| **Santa Ana** | **California** | Hot, dry; spreads wildfires |
| 🔥 **Kalbaishakhi (কালবৈশাখী, nor'wester)** | **Bangladesh**, West Bengal | Violent thunderstorms from the **north-west** in the **pre-monsoon (March–May)**, especially in Baishakh |

## Climate zones 🔥
- **Weather** = short-term condition of the atmosphere; **climate** = average weather over a long time (usually **30+ years**).
- **Köppen climate classification** (Wladimir Köppen) — main groups: **A** tropical, **B** dry, **C** temperate, **D** continental (cold), **E** polar.
- Simple heat zones: **Torrid zone** (between the tropics), **Temperate zones** (tropics to polar circles), **Frigid zones** (inside the polar circles).
- Mediterranean climate: **dry summers, rainy winters**.

## Bangladesh climate 🔥
- Bangladesh has a **tropical monsoon climate (ক্রান্তীয় মৌসুমি জলবায়ু)**.
- Three main seasons: **Summer / pre-monsoon (March–May)**, **Rainy / monsoon (June–October)**, **Winter (November–February)**. Culturally Bangladesh has **six seasons (ষড়ঋতু)**.
- About **70–80%** of the annual rain falls in the monsoon.
- Wettest area: **Lalakhal, Sylhet**; driest: **Lalpur, Natore**.
- Lowest recorded temperature: **2.6 °C at Srimangal (1968)**.

## World weather records and instruments
- **Wettest place:** **Mawsynram**, Meghalaya, India (Cherrapunji is close by). **Driest:** **Atacama Desert**, Chile.
- **Highest recorded temperature:** **Death Valley, USA** (56.7 °C, 1913). **Lowest:** **Vostok station, Antarctica** (−89.2 °C, 1983).
- Instruments: **barometer** (pressure), **anemometer** (wind speed), **wind vane** (direction), **hygrometer** (humidity), **rain gauge** (rainfall), **thermometer** (temperature).

## Quick revision
- Air: **N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%**, Ar 0.93%, CO₂ 0.04%.
- All weather: **troposphere**; ozone layer: **stratosphere**; meteors burn: **mesosphere**; radio waves reflected: **ionosphere (thermosphere)**.
- Temperature falls **6.5 °C per km** in the troposphere.
- Coriolis: right in the north, left in the south (**Ferrel's law**).
- **Roaring Forties** = westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere.
- Loo = India; Chinook = Rockies ("snow eater"); Harmattan = West Africa ("doctor").
- Bangladesh: **tropical monsoon**; **Kalbaishakhi** in March–May.
- Wettest place in Bangladesh: **Lalakhal**; driest: **Lalpur**.

GEO-03.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the largest/deepest ocean, the deepest trench, warm vs cold currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Humboldt), where warm and cold currents meet, and the causes of spring and neap tides.

## Oceans (মহাসাগর) 🔥
- Oceans cover about **71%** of Earth's surface and hold about **97%** of Earth's water.
- Earth has **five oceans** (largest → smallest):

| Rank | Ocean | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 🔥 **Pacific (প্রশান্ত মহাসাগর)** | **Largest and deepest**; covers about a third of Earth's surface; named by **Magellan** ("peaceful"). Deepest point: **Challenger Deep, Mariana Trench** (about **11,000 m**; figures vary from 10,935 to 11,034 m). **"Ring of Fire"** of volcanoes around it |
| 2 | **Atlantic** | **S-shaped**; **busiest ocean for trade**; deepest point: **Puerto Rico Trench** |
| 3 | 🔥 **Indian** | **Only ocean named after a country** (India); deepest point: **Java (Sunda) Trench**; the **Bay of Bengal** is part of it |
| 4 | **Southern (Antarctic)** | Surrounds Antarctica; recognised by the International Hydrographic Organization in **2000** |
| 5 | 🔥 **Arctic** | **Smallest and shallowest**; mostly frozen |

- **Largest bay:** **Bay of Bengal (বঙ্গোপসাগর)**. **Largest gulf:** **Gulf of Mexico**.
- **Sargasso Sea** (North Atlantic): the **only sea with no land coast** — bounded by ocean currents; full of floating **Sargassum** seaweed.
- **Average ocean salinity:** about **35 parts per thousand (35‰)**. The **Dead Sea** (really a lake) is among the saltiest water bodies; the **Red Sea** is the saltiest open sea.

### Ocean floor (relief)
**Continental shelf** (shallow, up to about 200 m deep; rich in fish, oil and gas) → **continental slope** → **deep-sea plain (abyssal plain)** → **ocean deeps/trenches**. **Mid-ocean ridges** are underwater mountain chains.
- **Swatch of No Ground (সোয়াচ অব নো গ্রাউন্ড):** a deep **submarine canyon** in the Bay of Bengal off Bangladesh; declared Bangladesh's **first marine protected area (2014)**.

### Law of the sea (UNCLOS, 1982)
| Zone | Width from the baseline |
|---|---|
| **Territorial sea** | **12 nautical miles** |
| **Contiguous zone** | **24 nautical miles** |
| 🔥 **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)** | **200 nautical miles** |
| Continental shelf | Up to 350 nautical miles (in some cases) |

- Bangladesh won its maritime boundary cases against **Myanmar (ITLOS, 2012)** and **India (Permanent Court of Arbitration, 2014)**, gaining about **1,18,813 sq km** of sea area.

## Ocean currents (সমুদ্রস্রোত) 🔥🔥
- Caused mainly by **planetary winds**, differences in **temperature and salinity (density)**, Earth's rotation (**Coriolis force**) and the shape of coasts.
- **Warm currents** flow from the **equator towards the poles**; **cold currents** flow from the **poles towards the equator**.
- In the Northern Hemisphere, currents move **clockwise**; in the Southern Hemisphere, **anti-clockwise**.

| Current | Warm/Cold | Ocean / location | Key fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Gulf Stream** | **Warm** | North Atlantic, from the Gulf of Mexico | Continues as the **North Atlantic Drift**; keeps **NW Europe's ports ice-free** |
| 🔥 **Kuroshio** (Japan current) | **Warm** | North Pacific, east of Japan | Called the **"Black Current"** |
| **Brazil, East Australian, Agulhas** | Warm | S. Atlantic, S. Pacific, Indian | |
| 🔥 **Labrador** | **Cold** | NW Atlantic, near Canada | **Meets the Gulf Stream near Newfoundland** → thick **fog** and the rich **Grand Banks** fishing ground |
| **Oyashio (Kurile)** | Cold | NW Pacific | **Meets the Kuroshio near Japan** → rich fishing |
| 🔥 **Humboldt (Peru)** | **Cold** | West coast of **South America** | Very rich fishery; helps create the **Atacama Desert** |
| **California** | Cold | West coast of the USA | |
| **Canary** | Cold | NW Africa | |
| **Benguela** | Cold | SW Africa | Linked to the **Namib Desert** |
| **West Australian** | Cold | Western Australia | |
| **Antarctic Circumpolar (West Wind Drift)** | Cold | Around Antarctica | **Largest ocean current** |

- 🔥 **Rule:** where **warm and cold currents meet**, there is **fog** and **rich fishing grounds** (plankton grow well).
- **Cold currents along west coasts** of continents in the tropics help form **hot deserts** (Atacama, Namib, Kalahari, Australian).
- **El Niño:** unusual **warming** of the eastern Pacific near Peru; brings drought to South Asia/Australia and floods to South America. **La Niña:** the opposite (cooling).
- **Indian Ocean currents reverse direction** with the monsoon seasons.

## Tides (জোয়ার-ভাটা) 🔥🔥
- The **regular rise and fall of sea level**, caused mainly by the **gravitational pull of the Moon** (and less by the Sun) and by Earth's rotation.
- The **Moon's tide-producing force is about 2.2 times the Sun's**, because the Moon is much closer.
- Most coasts get **two high tides and two low tides** in about **24 hours 50 minutes**. So a high tide comes about every **12 hours 25 minutes**, and the tide is about **50 minutes later** each day.
- **Primary tide (মুখ্য জোয়ার):** on the side facing the Moon. **Secondary tide (গৌণ জোয়ার):** on the opposite side (caused by centrifugal force).

| Type | When | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Spring tide (ভরা কটাল)** | **New moon (অমাবস্যা) and full moon (পূর্ণিমা)** — Sun, Moon and Earth **in a straight line** | **Highest high tides and lowest low tides** |
| 🔥 **Neap tide (মরা কটাল)** | **First and last quarter (অষ্টমী)** — Sun and Moon **at right angles** to Earth | **Smallest tidal range** |

- **Highest tidal range in the world:** **Bay of Fundy, Canada** (about 16 m).
- **Tidal bore (বান):** a wall of water that rushes up a river mouth at high tide (seen in the Meghna estuary).
- **Tides help** navigation into river ports (e.g. Kolkata, Mongla), fishing, and **tidal power**.

## Quick revision
- Largest and deepest ocean: **Pacific**; deepest point: **Challenger Deep, Mariana Trench**.
- Smallest ocean: **Arctic**; only ocean named after a country: **Indian**.
- Largest bay: **Bay of Bengal**; sea with no coast: **Sargasso Sea**.
- EEZ = **200 nautical miles**; territorial sea = **12 nautical miles**.
- Gulf Stream and Kuroshio = **warm**; Labrador, Humboldt, Canary, Benguela = **cold**.
- Gulf Stream + Labrador meet near **Newfoundland** → fog, fishing.
- Spring tide: **full/new moon**, all in a line; neap tide: **quarter moons**, right angle.
- Tides are caused mainly by the **Moon**.

GEO-04.notes:
> **Why it matters:** "Largest / longest / highest / deepest" questions are among the most common geography MCQs in every Bangladeshi exam. Learn the tables; where sources disagree, the usual exam answer is given with a note.

## Rivers 🔥
| Record | River | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Longest river in the world** | **Nile** (Africa), about **6,650 km** | Some recent studies claim the **Amazon** is longer; exams accept **Nile** |
| 🔥 **Largest river by volume/discharge and basin** | **Amazon** (South America) | Carries the most water of any river |
| Longest river in **Asia** | **Yangtze (Chang Jiang)**, China, about 6,300 km | 3rd longest in the world |
| Longest in **North America** | **Mississippi–Missouri** | |
| Longest in **Europe** | **Volga** (Russia) | Flows into the Caspian Sea |
| Longest in **Australia** | **Murray** (Murray–Darling system) | |
| River through the **most countries** | **Danube** (Europe, 10 countries) | |
| **Deepest river** | **Congo** (Africa) | **Crosses the equator twice** |
| 🔥 **Largest delta** | **Ganges–Brahmaputra delta (Bengal delta)** | Bangladesh and West Bengal |
| **Sorrow rivers** | Huang He (Yellow River) = **"Sorrow of China"**; Damodar = "Sorrow of Bengal" | |

## Mountains and peaks 🔥🔥
| Record | Name | Height (approx.) / notes |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Highest peak** | **Mount Everest** (Nepal–China border) | **8,848.86 m** (Nepal–China joint measurement, **2020**; older books give **8,848 m**). Nepali name **Sagarmatha**; Tibetan **Chomolungma**. First climbed on **29 May 1953** by **Edmund Hillary & Tenzing Norgay** |
| 🔥 **2nd highest** | **K2 (Godwin-Austen)**, Pakistan–China (Karakoram) | About **8,611 m** |
| **3rd highest** | **Kangchenjunga** (Nepal–India) | About 8,586 m |
| Highest in **South America** (and outside Asia) | **Aconcagua** (Argentina, Andes) | About 6,961 m |
| Highest in **North America** | **Denali** (Mount McKinley), Alaska | About 6,190 m |
| Highest in **Africa** | **Kilimanjaro** (Tanzania) | About 5,895 m; a dormant volcano |
| Highest in **Europe** | **Elbrus** (Russia, Caucasus) | About 5,642 m (Mont Blanc is highest in the Alps/Western Europe) |
| Highest in **Antarctica** | **Vinson Massif** | About 4,892 m |
| Highest in **Oceania** | **Puncak Jaya** (Indonesia) | About 4,884 m; **Kosciuszko** is highest on mainland Australia |
| **Tallest from base** | **Mauna Kea** (Hawaii) | Over 10,000 m from the ocean floor |
| 🔥 **Longest mountain range** | **Andes** (South America) | About 7,000 km |
| **Highest mountain range** | **Himalayas** | Young **fold mountains** |
| 🔥 **"Roof of the World"** | **Pamir Plateau** (Central Asia) | **Tibetan Plateau** is the highest and largest plateau |

- **First Bangladeshi to climb Everest:** **Musa Ibrahim (2010)**. **First Bangladeshi woman:** **Nishat Majumder (2012)**.
- **Highest peak of Bangladesh:** **Saka Haphong** (Bandarban) is the highest by most modern measurements (about **1,052 m**); officially and in older books, **Tajingdong (Bijoy)** or **Keokradong** are named. See GEO-05.

## Deserts 🔥
| Record | Desert | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Largest desert overall** | **Antarctic Desert** | A **cold desert** (very low precipitation) |
| 🔥 **Largest hot desert** | **Sahara** (North Africa) | About **9 million sq km**; the usual exam answer for "largest desert" |
| 2nd largest hot desert | **Arabian Desert** | Includes the **Rub' al Khali (Empty Quarter)** |
| Largest in **Asia** | **Gobi** (Mongolia–China) | A **cold desert** |
| 🔥 **Driest desert** | **Atacama** (Chile) | Some places have had no recorded rain for years |
| **Kalahari** | Southern Africa (Botswana) | |
| **Namib** | Namibia | One of the oldest deserts |

GEO-05.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the three physiographic divisions of Bangladesh with their shares (12% / 8% / 80%), the Pleistocene terraces (Barind, Madhupur, Lalmai), the highest peak, haors and beels, and soil types (red soil, alluvial, peat, saline).

## Basic facts
- Bangladesh is mostly part of the **world's largest delta**, the **Bengal (Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna) delta**.
- Area: **1,47,570 sq km** (the official figure used in most textbooks; some BBS sources give about **1,48,460 sq km**).
- Most of the land is **less than 10 m above sea level**; the land generally **slopes from north to south**.

## Three physiographic divisions (NCTB) 🔥🔥
| Division | Share of area | Age | Areas |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Tertiary hills (টারশিয়ারি যুগের পাহাড়সমূহ)** | **About 12%** | Formed in the **Tertiary period**, when the Himalayas rose | South-eastern and north/north-eastern hills |
| 🔥 **Pleistocene terraces (প্লাইস্টোসিনকালের চত্বরভূমি)** | **About 8%** | About **25,000 years** old (Pleistocene) | **Barind Tract, Madhupur & Bhawal Tract, Lalmai Hills** |
| 🔥 **Recent floodplains (সাম্প্রতিক কালের প্লাবন সমভূমি)** | **About 80%** | Most recent; built by river silt | Most of the country |

### 1. Tertiary hills
| Group | Districts / facts |
|---|---|
| **South-eastern hills (দক্ষিণ-পূর্বাঞ্চলের পাহাড়সমূহ)** | **Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Bandarban** (Chittagong Hill Tracts), **Chattogram, Cox's Bazar**. Made of sandstone, siltstone and shale; average height about 600 m |
| **North and north-eastern hills (উত্তর ও উত্তর-পূর্বাঞ্চলের পাহাড়সমূহ)** | Northern **Mymensingh and Netrokona** (Garo hills area), **Sylhet, Moulvibazar, Habiganj**. Local hills are called **"টিলা" (tila)** in Sylhet |

- 🔥 **Highest peak:** textbooks and official sources name **Tajingdong (তাজিংডং), also called Bijoy (বিজয়)**, in **Bandarban**. Older books named **Keokradong (কেওক্রাডং)**. Modern GPS surveys show **Saka Haphong (সাকা হাফং / Mowdok Mual), Bandarban**, about **1,052 m**, to be the highest. **In exams, give Tajingdong (Bijoy) unless Saka Haphong is among the options and Tajingdong is not.**
- **Chimbuk** hill and **Nilgiri** are in Bandarban; **Sitakunda's Chandranath hill** is in Chattogram.

### 2. Pleistocene terraces 🔥
| Terrace | Area | Location / soil |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Barind Tract (বরেন্দ্রভূমি)** | **About 9,320 sq km** — **largest** terrace | Greater **Rajshahi, Dinajpur, Rangpur, Bogura**, Joypurhat, Naogaon; **reddish/grey** clay soil; **dry, low rainfall** |
| 🔥 **Madhupur and Bhawal Tract (মধুপুর ও ভাওয়ালের গড়)** | **About 4,103 sq km** | **Tangail, Gazipur**, Mymensingh; **red and brown soil (লালচে মাটি)**; sal forest |
| **Lalmai Hills (লালমাই পাহাড়)** | **About 34 sq km** — smallest | **Cumilla**; reddish soil with sand and gravel; Mainamati Buddhist ruins nearby |

- The soils of these terraces are **red or reddish-brown** because of **iron oxide**, and are **acidic**.

### 3. Recent floodplains 🔥
Formed by the **Padma (Ganges), Jamuna (Brahmaputra), Meghna, Teesta** and their branches. NCTB divides them into:
- **Piedmont (foothill) plain (পাদদেশীয় সমভূমি):** **Rangpur–Dinajpur**, formed by rivers from the Himalayan foothills.
- **Floodplains (প্লাবন সমভূমি):** along the major rivers — flooded every year, very fertile.
- **Deltaic plain (ব-দ্বীপ সমভূমি):** **Kushtia, Jashore, Faridpur, Khulna** region.
- **Sylhet basin (সিলেট অববাহিকা):** low bowl-shaped land with **haors**.
- **Cumilla plain**, **Chattogram coastal plain**, and **tidal/coastal plains (স্রোতজ ও উপকূলীয় সমভূমি)** in the south (Khulna, Barishal, Patuakhali, Noakhali).

### Haors, beels and wetlands 🔥
| Feature | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Haor (হাওর)** | Large **bowl-shaped depression**, flooded in the monsoon; mostly in **Sunamganj, Sylhet, Moulvibazar, Habiganj, Netrokona, Kishoreganj, Brahmanbaria** |
| 🔥 **Hakaluki Haor** | **Largest haor** of Bangladesh (Moulvibazar–Sylhet) |
| 🔥 **Tanguar Haor** | Sunamganj; Bangladesh's **2nd Ramsar site (2000)** |
| **Beel (বিল)** | Smaller low-lying water body |
| 🔥 **Chalan Beel (চলন বিল)** | **Largest beel** — Pabna, Natore, Sirajganj |
| **Arial Beel** | Dhaka–Munshiganj |

## Soils of Bangladesh 🔥
| Soil type | Where | Features |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Floodplain (alluvial) soil — পলি মাটি** | **About 80% of the country** | **Most fertile**; renewed by silt every flood; best for **rice and jute** |
| 🔥 **Terrace soil (red/brown soil — লাল মাটি)** | **Barind, Madhupur, Lalmai** | Red/reddish-brown (iron oxide), **acidic**, less fertile; good for jackfruit, pineapple, sal trees |
| **Hill soil (পাহাড়ি মাটি)** | Chittagong Hill Tracts, Sylhet hills | Acidic, sandy/loamy, erodes easily; good for **tea** (Sylhet), fruit; **jhum** (shifting) cultivation |
| **Peat soil (পিট/জৈব মাটি)** | **Gopalganj, Khulna** low basins (e.g. Baghia beel), parts of the Sylhet basin | Very high in organic matter; waterlogged |
| **Saline soil (লবণাক্ত মাটি)** | **Coastal districts: Satkhira, Khulna, Bagerhat**, Patuakhali, Barguna | Salt from sea water; reduces crop yield; increasing with sea-level rise |
| **Acid sulphate soil** | Parts of the coast, Chattogram and Cox's Bazar mangrove areas | Very acidic when drained |

- **By texture:** **sandy (বেলে)**, **loamy (দোআঁশ)** — **best for farming**, and **clay (এঁটেল)**. Loam is a mix of sand, silt and clay.
- **SRDI (Soil Resource Development Institute)** carries out soil surveys in Bangladesh.

## Quick revision
- Divisions: **Tertiary hills 12%**, **Pleistocene terraces 8%**, **Recent floodplains 80%**.
- Pleistocene terraces: **Barind (largest, ~9,320 sq km)**, **Madhupur–Bhawal (~4,103 sq km)**, **Lalmai (~34 sq km, Cumilla)**.
- Terraces are about **25,000 years** old, with **red soil**.
- Highest peak: **Tajingdong (Bijoy)** in textbooks; Saka Haphong in modern surveys.
- Largest haor: **Hakaluki**; largest beel: **Chalan Beel**.
- Most fertile soil: **alluvial floodplain soil**; peat soil: **Gopalganj/Khulna**; saline soil: **coastal south-west**.
- Best soil texture for crops: **loam (দোআঁশ)**.

GEO-06.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who coined "ecosystem", the parts of a food chain, levels of biodiversity, IUCN categories, and Bangladesh facts: the Sundarbans (World Heritage and Ramsar site), Ramsar sites, national parks, ECAs and St. Martin's Island.

## Ecosystem (বাস্তুতন্ত্র) 🔥
- An **ecosystem** is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their **non-living environment**.
- 🔥 The term **"ecosystem"** was coined by **Arthur G. Tansley** (British ecologist) in **1935**.
- **Ecology:** the study of relationships between organisms and their environment; the word was coined by **Ernst Haeckel** (1866).

| Component | Examples / role |
|---|---|
| **Abiotic (অজীব)** | Sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature, minerals |
| 🔥 **Producers (উৎপাদক)** | **Green plants, algae** — make food by **photosynthesis** |
| **Primary consumers** | **Herbivores** (deer, grasshopper, zooplankton) |
| **Secondary / tertiary consumers** | **Carnivores** (frog, snake, tiger) |
| 🔥 **Decomposers (বিয়োজক)** | **Bacteria and fungi** — break down dead matter and return nutrients to soil |

- **Food chain:** grass → deer → tiger. **Food web:** many connected food chains.
- **Trophic level:** each step in a food chain.
- 🔥 **10% law (Lindeman, 1942):** only about **10% of energy** passes from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost mostly as heat.
- The **Sun** is the ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems.
- **Types:** terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, river, sea, wetland).

## Biodiversity (জীববৈচিত্র্য) 🔥
- The **variety of life** on Earth. The word **"biodiversity"** was coined by **Walter G. Rosen** (1985) and popularised by **E. O. Wilson**.
- 🔥 **Three levels:** **genetic diversity**, **species diversity**, **ecosystem diversity**.
- **Biodiversity hotspot:** a region with very high species richness that is seriously threatened; idea by **Norman Myers (1988)**. Bangladesh is in the **Indo-Burma hotspot**.
- **Conservation:**
  - **In-situ (স্বস্থানে):** protecting species **in their natural habitat** — national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves.
  - **Ex-situ (স্থানান্তরে):** **outside** the natural habitat — **zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks**.
- **Endemic species:** found only in one place.

### IUCN Red List categories 🔥
**IUCN** (International Union for Conservation of Nature), founded **1948**, headquarters **Gland, Switzerland**, publishes the **Red List** of threatened species.
Order: **Extinct (EX) → Extinct in the Wild (EW) → Critically Endangered (CR) → Endangered (EN) → Vulnerable (VU) → Near Threatened (NT) → Least Concern (LC)**; plus **Data Deficient (DD)**.
- **Threatened** = CR + EN + VU.

## National symbols of Bangladesh
| Symbol | Name |
|---|---|
| 🔥 National animal | **Royal Bengal Tiger** |
| National bird | **Magpie robin (দোয়েল)** |
| National fish | **Hilsa (ইলিশ)** |
| National flower | **Water lily (শাপলা)** |
| National tree | **Mango tree** |
| National fruit | **Jackfruit** |

## The Sundarbans (সুন্দরবন) 🔥🔥
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Type | **World's largest single tract of mangrove forest** |
| Total area | About **10,000 sq km**; about **62%** (about **6,017 sq km**) is in **Bangladesh**, the rest in India |
| Districts (Bangladesh) | Mainly **Khulna, Satkhira, Bagerhat** (with small parts of Patuakhali and Barguna) |
| Name | Usually said to come from the **Sundari tree** (*Heritiera fomes*) |
| 🔥 **UNESCO World Heritage Site** | **1997** — Bangladesh's **only natural** World Heritage site |
| 🔥 **Ramsar site** | **1992** — Bangladesh's **first Ramsar site** |
| Famous animals | **Royal Bengal Tiger**, spotted deer, estuarine crocodile, Irrawaddy and Ganges dolphins |
| Tiger count | **125** tigers in the Bangladesh Sundarbans (survey results announced in **2024**; the previous count was 114) |

> 🔄 Update: tiger numbers change with each survey; check the latest Forest Department figure.

## Protected areas of Bangladesh 🔥
**Main laws:** **Bangladesh Wildlife (Conservation and Security) Act 2012**; **Bangladesh Biodiversity Act 2017**; **Environment Conservation Act 1995** (for ECAs).

### Ramsar sites (2)
1. 🔥 **Sundarbans** — **1992** (first)
2. 🔥 **Tanguar Haor** (Sunamganj) — **2000**

### Selected national parks (জাতীয় উদ্যান)
| National park | District | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Bhawal National Park** | **Gazipur** | One of the oldest and best-known |
| **Madhupur National Park** | Tangail | Sal forest |
| 🔥 **Lawachara National Park** | **Moulvibazar** | Rainforest; home of the **Hoolock gibbon** (only ape of Bangladesh) |
| **Himchari National Park** | Cox's Bazar | Hills and waterfalls by the sea |
| **Satchari National Park** | Habiganj | |
| **Ramsagar National Park** | Dinajpur | Around the large Ramsagar dighi |
| **Nijhum Dwip National Park** | Noakhali | Island; spotted deer |
| **Kaptai National Park** | Rangamati | |

### Selected wildlife sanctuaries (বন্যপ্রাণী অভয়ারণ্য)
**Rema-Kalenga** (Habiganj), **Char Kukri-Mukri** (Bhola), **Pablakhali** (Rangamati), **Chunati** (Chattogram), **Teknaf** (Cox's Bazar), and the three sanctuaries inside the Sundarbans (East, West and South).
- **Safari parks:** **Dulahazra, Cox's Bazar** (the first, 1999) and **Gazipur**.

### Ecologically Critical Areas (ECA — পরিবেশগতভাবে সংকটাপন্ন এলাকা) 🔥
Declared under the **Environment Conservation Act 1995**. The first **eight ECAs (1999)** were:
**Sundarbans** (10 km around it), **Cox's Bazar–Teknaf beach**, 🔥 **St. Martin's Island**, **Sonadia Island**, **Hakaluki Haor**, **Tanguar Haor**, **Marjat Baor** (Jhenaidah), and **Gulshan–Baridhara Lake** (Dhaka). More were added later (e.g. rivers around Dhaka).

### Marine and island facts
- 🔥 **St. Martin's Island (সেন্ট মার্টিন দ্বীপ / নারিকেল জিঞ্জিরা):** Bangladesh's **only coral island**, in Teknaf, Cox's Bazar.
- **Swatch of No Ground:** Bangladesh's **first marine protected area (2014)** — whales, dolphins, sharks.

## Quick revision
- "Ecosystem" coined by **Tansley (1935)**; "ecology" by **Haeckel**.
- Producers = green plants; decomposers = **bacteria and fungi**.
- **10% energy law** (Lindeman).
- Biodiversity levels: **genetic, species, ecosystem**.
- IUCN HQ: **Gland, Switzerland**; Red List.
- Sundarbans: World Heritage **1997**, Ramsar **1992**; ~62% in Bangladesh.
- Ramsar sites of Bangladesh: **Sundarbans, Tanguar Haor**.
- Lawachara: **Hoolock gibbon**; St. Martin's: **only coral island**.
- ECAs are declared under the **Environment Conservation Act 1995**.

GEO-07.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the greenhouse gases, the main greenhouse gas, the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement years, IPCC facts, where COP meetings were held, the ozone layer and CFCs, and Bangladesh's climate vulnerability. This topic is also central in BCS written papers.

## Greenhouse effect and global warming 🔥
- **Greenhouse effect (গ্রিনহাউস প্রভাব):** some gases in the atmosphere let sunlight in but **trap the heat (infrared radiation)** that Earth gives off, keeping the planet warm. Without it, Earth would be about **−18 °C** on average instead of about **15 °C**.
- **Global warming (বৈশ্বিক উষ্ণায়ন):** the rise in Earth's average temperature because humans add extra greenhouse gases, mainly by **burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, gas) and **deforestation**.
- **Joseph Fourier** described the effect (1820s); **Svante Arrhenius** (1896) first calculated how CO₂ warms Earth.

### Greenhouse gases 🔥🔥
| Gas | Main sources | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Carbon dioxide (CO₂)** | Burning fossil fuels, deforestation, cement | **Largest contributor** to human-caused warming |
| 🔥 **Methane (CH₄)** | **Paddy fields**, livestock, landfills, gas leaks | Far more powerful per molecule than CO₂ (about 28 times over 100 years) |
| **Nitrous oxide (N₂O)** | **Chemical fertiliser**, industry | |
| **CFCs, HFCs, PFCs** | Refrigerators, ACs, aerosols | Very powerful; CFCs also destroy ozone |
| **Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆)** | Electrical equipment | **Highest global warming potential** |
| **Water vapour** | Natural evaporation | **Most abundant** greenhouse gas (a feedback, not directly controlled) |

- **Kyoto Protocol's six gases:** CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆.
- Earth has warmed by about **1.1–1.2 °C** above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels; **2024** was the **warmest year on record** and the first calendar year about **1.5 °C** above pre-industrial levels (WMO).

> 🔄 Update: temperature records and CO₂ levels are broken almost every year; check the latest WMO report.

### Effects
- **Sea-level rise** (melting glaciers and ice sheets, thermal expansion of sea water), more intense **cyclones**, floods and droughts, heatwaves, **salinity intrusion**, coral bleaching, loss of species, **climate refugees**.
- **Mitigation (প্রশমন)** = reducing emissions (renewable energy, forests). **Adaptation (অভিযোজন)** = adjusting to impacts (embankments, saline-tolerant rice, floating gardens).
- **Carbon sink:** absorbs CO₂ (forests, oceans). **Net zero / carbon neutral:** emissions balanced by removals. **Carbon credit:** a permit to emit one tonne of CO₂ that can be traded.

## Global climate institutions and agreements 🔥🔥
| Item | Key facts |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **IPCC** (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) | Set up in **1988** by **WMO and UNEP**; HQ **Geneva**; shared the **2007 Nobel Peace Prize** with **Al Gore**. Latest full cycle: **Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), 2021–2023** |
| 🔥 **UNFCCC** (UN Framework Convention on Climate Change) | Adopted at the **Rio Earth Summit, 1992**; in force **1994**; secretariat in **Bonn, Germany**. Its yearly meeting is the **COP** (Conference of the Parties); **COP1: Berlin, 1995** |
| 🔥 **Kyoto Protocol** | Adopted at **COP3, Kyoto (Japan), 1997**; in force **2005**; **binding emission cuts for developed (Annex I) countries**; introduced carbon trading and the **Clean Development Mechanism (CDM)** |
| 🔥 **Paris Agreement** | Adopted at **COP21, Paris, December 2015**; in force **4 November 2016**. Goal: keep warming **well below 2 °C** and try to limit it to **1.5 °C**; every country submits **NDCs** (Nationally Determined Contributions) |

### Recent COPs
| COP | Place | Year | Key outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| COP26 | **Glasgow**, UK | 2021 | Glasgow Climate Pact; "phase down" coal |
| COP27 | **Sharm el-Sheikh**, Egypt | 2022 | 🔥 Agreement to set up a **Loss and Damage Fund** |
| COP28 | **Dubai**, UAE | 2023 | Loss and Damage Fund made operational; first call to "**transition away from fossil fuels**" |
| COP29 | **Baku**, Azerbaijan | 2024 | New climate-finance goal: at least **US$300 billion a year by 2035** for developing countries |
| COP30 | **Belém**, Brazil | 2025 | Held in the Amazon region |

> 🔄 Update: check the venue and results of the latest COP.

## Bangladesh and climate change 🔥
- Bangladesh is one of the **most climate-vulnerable countries** because of its low, flat delta, dense population and cyclone-prone coast.
- A **1 m sea-level rise** could flood about **17–18%** of Bangladesh's land (the commonly cited estimate).
- **BCCSAP** (Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan): **2009** — among the first such plans in developing countries.
- **Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund** (from the country's own budget): set up in **2009–10** under the **Climate Change Trust Act 2010**.
- **National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2023–2050**: submitted to the UNFCCC in **2022**.
- Bangladesh has chaired the **Climate Vulnerable Forum (CVF)**.
- Adaptation examples: **floating gardens (ভাসমান বাগান)**, saline-tolerant rice (e.g. BRRI varieties), cyclone shelters, raised homesteads.

## Ozone layer (ওজোন স্তর) 🔥🔥
- **Ozone (O₃)** is a molecule of **three oxygen atoms**. The **ozone layer** is in the **stratosphere** (about **15–35 km**).
- It **absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV-B and UV-C) rays** that cause **skin cancer, cataracts** and crop damage.
- Measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**. An **"ozone hole"** means ozone below **220 DU**.
- 🔥 The **ozone hole over Antarctica** was reported in **1985** by scientists of the **British Antarctic Survey**. It is worst in the southern **spring (September–October)**.
- 🔥 **Main ozone-depleting substances:** **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons)** — used in **refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays, foam**; also **halons** (fire extinguishers), carbon tetrachloride, methyl bromide. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
- **Mario Molina, Sherwood Rowland and Paul Crutzen** won the **1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for their work on ozone depletion.
- **Ground-level ozone** is a harmful **air pollutant** (part of smog), unlike stratospheric ozone.

| Treaty | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Vienna Convention** for the Protection of the Ozone Layer | **1985** | Framework treaty |
| 🔥 **Montreal Protocol** | **16 September 1987** (in force 1989) | **Phases out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances**; the first UN treaty ratified by **every UN member state**; seen as the most successful environmental treaty |
| **Kigali Amendment** | **2016** (Kigali, Rwanda) | Phases **down HFCs** (which don't harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases) |

- **16 September = International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer.**
- The ozone layer is **recovering**; it is expected to return to 1980 levels around the middle of this century.

## Important days
**5 June — World Environment Day** (first held **1974**, set up after the 1972 Stockholm Conference); **22 April — Earth Day**; **16 September — Ozone Day**; **23 March — World Meteorological Day**.

## Quick revision
- Main human greenhouse gas: **CO₂**; methane from **paddy fields and livestock**; most abundant GHG: **water vapour**.
- IPCC: **1988**, WMO + UNEP, Nobel **2007**.
- UNFCCC: **Rio 1992**; Kyoto Protocol: **1997** (in force 2005); Paris Agreement: **2015** (in force 2016).
- Paris goal: **well below 2 °C, aim 1.5 °C**; countries submit **NDCs**.
- Loss and Damage Fund agreed at **COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022)**.
- Ozone layer: **stratosphere**, absorbs **UV**; unit **Dobson**.
- CFCs destroy ozone; **Montreal Protocol 1987**; **Kigali Amendment 2016** (HFCs).
- BCCSAP **2009**; NAP **2023–2050**.

GEO-08.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Bangladesh is one of the most disaster-prone countries, so exams ask the names of cyclones in different regions, the deadliest cyclones (1970, 1991, Sidr, Aila, Amphan, Remal), port signal numbers, types of floods, the Richter scale and seismic waves, and landslide/drought-prone areas.

## Hazard vs disaster
- **Hazard (দুর্যোগের ঝুঁকি/আপদ):** a natural or human-made event that *can* cause harm (e.g. a cyclone at sea).
- **Disaster (দুর্যোগ):** when a hazard seriously harms people, property and livelihoods beyond a community's ability to cope.
- **Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability** (reduced by capacity).
- **Natural disasters:** cyclone, flood, earthquake, drought, landslide, tsunami, lightning. **Human-made:** fire, building collapse, industrial accidents.
- 🔥 In Bangladesh, **lightning (বজ্রপাত)** was **declared a natural disaster in 2016**.

## Cyclone (ঘূর্ণিঝড়) 🔥🔥
- A strong **low-pressure** storm with winds **spiralling inwards** — **anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere**, clockwise in the Southern.
- Forms over **warm seas (about 26–27 °C or more)**; the calm centre is the **eye (চোখ)**.
- **Storm surge (জলোচ্ছ্বাস):** the rise of sea water pushed onto land by cyclone winds — the **biggest killer** in coastal Bangladesh.

| Name | Region |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Cyclone** | **Indian Ocean / Bay of Bengal** |
| 🔥 **Hurricane** | **Atlantic** and north-east Pacific (USA, Caribbean) |
| 🔥 **Typhoon** | **North-west Pacific** (China, Japan, Philippines) |
| **Willy-willy** | Old name in **Australia** |
| **Tornado** | Small, very violent twister over land (USA) |

- Cyclones in the North Indian Ocean are named from a list prepared by **13 countries** (WMO/ESCAP Panel), including Bangladesh.

**Bangladesh wind classification (BMD / IMD):** depression (31–49 km/h) → deep depression (50–61) → **cyclonic storm (62–88)** → **severe cyclonic storm (89–117)** → very severe (118–165) → extremely severe (166–220) → **super cyclonic storm (221 km/h or more)**.

### Sea-port warning signals 🔥
| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1, 2 | **Distant** cautionary / warning |
| 3, 4 | **Local** cautionary / warning |
| 5, 6, 7 | **Danger** |
| 🔥 **8, 9, 10** | **Great danger (মহাবিপদ সংকেত)** |
| **11** | **Communication failure** with the warning centre |

- River ports use a separate system of **signals 1–4**.

### Major cyclones in Bangladesh 🔥
| Date | Name / area | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **12 November 1970** | **Bhola cyclone** | **Deadliest** recorded tropical cyclone in the world: about **3–5 lakh** deaths |
| 🔥 **29 April 1991** | Chattogram–Cox's Bazar coast | About **1.4 lakh** deaths |
| 🔥 **15 November 2007** | **Sidr (সিডর)** | Super cyclone; south-west coast and Sundarbans; more than 3,000 deaths |
| **25 May 2009** | **Aila (আইলা)** | Khulna–Satkhira; long-term saline flooding |
| 2019 | **Fani**, **Bulbul** | |
| **20 May 2020** | **Amphan (আম্পান)** | Super cyclone; south-west coast |
| 2021 | **Yaas** | |
| May 2023 | **Mocha** | Cox's Bazar–Myanmar coast |
| **May 2024** | **Remal (রেমাল)** | Khulna–Barishal coast |

## Flood (বন্যা) 🔥
| Type | Where / cause |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Flash flood (আকস্মিক বন্যা)** | **Sylhet–Sunamganj haor region** and hill areas; heavy rain in upstream hills (Meghalaya, Tripura); water rises within hours; damages **Boro rice** in April–May |
| **Monsoon / riverine flood** | Overflow of the Padma, Jamuna, Meghna in **July–September** |
| **Rain-fed flood** | Heavy local rain with poor drainage (e.g. urban waterlogging in Dhaka, Chattogram) |
| **Tidal / storm-surge flood** | Coastal areas, during cyclones and spring tides |

- 🔥 **Major floods:** **1988** (about 60% of the country flooded) and **1998** (about two-thirds flooded, lasted more than two months — the longest); also 2004, 2007, **2022** (Sylhet flash flood), **August 2024** (Feni, Cumilla, Noakhali and other eastern districts).
- Normal floods (**বর্ষা**) bring fertile silt; damaging floods are **বন্যা**.

## Earthquake (ভূমিকম্প) 🔥
- Sudden shaking of the ground caused mainly by movement along **faults / tectonic plate boundaries**.
- **Focus (hypocentre):** point inside the Earth where it starts. 🔥 **Epicentre (উপকেন্দ্র):** point on the surface **directly above the focus** — greatest damage.
- 🔥 Recorded by a **seismograph**. **Magnitude** (energy) on the **Richter scale** (Charles Richter, 1935; now mostly the **moment magnitude scale**); **intensity** (damage) on the **Modified Mercalli scale (I–XII)**. Each whole number on the Richter scale = about **10 times** larger amplitude (about 32 times more energy).

| Seismic wave | Feature |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **P-wave (primary)** | **Fastest**; arrives first; travels through **solids, liquids and gases** |
| **S-wave (secondary)** | Slower; travels **only through solids** (shows Earth's outer core is liquid) |
| **Surface (L) waves** | Slowest; **most destructive** |

- **Bangladesh risk:** highest in the **north and north-east (Sylhet, Mymensingh, Rangpur)** and the Chattogram hill region, close to the Dauki fault and the Indian–Burmese plate boundary. **Dhaka** is highly vulnerable because of dense, poorly built buildings.
- **Great Indian (Assam) earthquake of 1897** (about magnitude 8) badly hit this region.
- **Tsunami (সুনামি):** Japanese for **"harbour wave"**; giant sea waves usually caused by **undersea earthquakes**. **26 December 2004** Indian Ocean tsunami (Sumatra, magnitude about 9.1) killed over 2 lakh people; **March 2011** Japan tsunami caused the **Fukushima** nuclear accident.

## Landslide (ভূমিধস) 🔥
- Mass movement of soil and rock down a slope.
- **Prone areas:** **Chattogram, Rangamati, Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Cox's Bazar** (including Rohingya camps).
- **Causes:** **heavy monsoon rain**, **hill cutting**, deforestation, settlement on slopes.
- **11 June 2007:** Chattogram city landslides, about **127** deaths. 🔥 **13 June 2017:** Rangamati and nearby districts, about **160** deaths — the deadliest landslide disaster in Bangladesh.

## Drought (খরা) 🔥
- A long period of **very low rainfall** causing water shortage.
- **Types:** meteorological (less rain), agricultural (soil moisture too low for crops), hydrological (rivers, groundwater fall).
- 🔥 **Most drought-prone:** **north-west Bangladesh — Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Naogaon (Barind Tract)**, Natore, Dinajpur.
- Reduced dry-season flow of the Ganges after the **Farakka Barrage (1975)** worsened drought and salinity in the south-west.

## Other hazards in Bangladesh
**River erosion (নদীভাঙন)** — especially along the **Jamuna and Padma**; **salinity intrusion** in the south-west coast; **cold waves**, **heatwaves**, **arsenic** in groundwater, **fire**, and building collapse (**Rana Plaza, 24 April 2013**).

## Quick revision
- Cyclone (Indian Ocean), hurricane (Atlantic), typhoon (NW Pacific), willy-willy (Australia).
- Deadliest cyclone: **12 November 1970** (Bhola); **29 April 1991**; **Sidr 2007**; **Aila 2009**; **Amphan 2020**; **Remal 2024**.
- Great danger signals: **8, 9, 10**; signal 11 = communication failure.
- Flash floods: **Sylhet haor region**; worst floods: **1988, 1998**.
- Richter scale = **magnitude**; Mercalli = **intensity**; seismograph records quakes.
- P-wave fastest; surface waves most destructive.
- Deadliest landslide: **13 June 2017**, Rangamati.
- Drought: **north-west (Barind)**; lightning declared disaster in **2016**.

GEO-09.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the stages of the disaster management cycle, what the Standing Orders on Disaster (SOD) are and their years, who heads the national and district committees, the Disaster Management Act 2012, the Cyclone Preparedness Programme, and the Sendai Framework.

## Disaster management cycle (দুর্যোগ ব্যবস্থাপনা চক্র) 🔥🔥
Disaster management is a **continuous cycle** of activities **before, during and after** a disaster.

| Stage | Phase | Activities |
|---|---|---|
| **Before** | 🔥 **Mitigation / prevention (প্রশমন)** | Reduce the **long-term risk**: embankments, cyclone shelters, building codes, afforestation, land-use planning |
| **Before** | 🔥 **Preparedness (প্রস্তুতি)** | Get ready: **early warning**, evacuation plans, drills, stockpiling food and medicine, volunteer training |
| **During / just after** | 🔥 **Response (সাড়া প্রদান)** | **Rescue**, evacuation, emergency relief (food, water, shelter), first aid |
| **After** | 🔥 **Recovery (পুনরুদ্ধার)** | **Rehabilitation (পুনর্বাসন)** and **reconstruction (পুনর্গঠন)**; "build back better" |

- Memory hook: **M-P-R-R** — **M**itigation → **P**reparedness → **R**esponse → **R**ecovery.
- **Risk reduction** (mitigation + preparedness) is now given more importance than relief alone — the approach Bangladesh follows (**comprehensive disaster management**).

## Legal and policy framework in Bangladesh 🔥
| Instrument | Year / fact |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Standing Orders on Disaster (SOD) — দুর্যোগ বিষয়ক স্থায়ী আদেশাবলি** | First issued **1997**; revised **2010**; latest **2019**. Sets out the **roles and responsibilities** of ministries, departments, committees (national to union level), NGOs and volunteers **before, during and after** disasters |
| 🔥 **Disaster Management Act 2012 (দুর্যোগ ব্যবস্থাপনা আইন, ২০১২)** | Gave legal basis to disaster management; created the **Department of Disaster Management (DDM)** |
| **National Disaster Management Policy** | **2015** |
| **National Plan for Disaster Management (NPDM)** | Five-year plans, e.g. **2021–2025** |

## Institutions 🔥
| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR)** | Lead ministry for disasters |
| **Department of Disaster Management (DDM)** | Implementing agency under MoDMR (formed under the 2012 Act) |
| **National Disaster Management Council (NDMC)** | 🔥 **Highest policy body**, headed by the **Head of Government (Prime Minister)** |
| **Inter-Ministerial Disaster Management Coordination Committee (IMDMCC)** | Headed by the **Minister for Disaster Management and Relief**; coordinates ministries |
| 🔥 **District Disaster Management Committee (DDMC)** | Headed by the **Deputy Commissioner (DC)** |
| **Upazila, Pourashava and City Corporation DMCs** | Coordinate at local level (City Corporation DMC headed by the **Mayor**) |
| 🔥 **Union Disaster Management Committee (UDMC)** | Headed by the **Union Parishad Chairman** |
| **National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC)** | Round-the-clock coordination during disasters |

## Early warning systems 🔥🔥
| Agency / system | Job |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD)** | **Weather and cyclone forecasts and warnings**; runs the **Storm Warning Centre (SWC)** and issues port signals |
| 🔥 **Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC)** | **Flood forecasts**; under the **Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB)**; set up in **1972** |
| **SPARRSO** (Space Research and Remote Sensing Organization) | Satellite images for cyclones, floods and crops |
| 🔥 **Cyclone Preparedness Programme (CPP)** | Joint programme of the **Government and the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society**, started in **1972** after the 1970 cyclone. Tens of thousands of trained **volunteers (about half women)** spread warnings using **megaphones, sirens and signal flags**, and help evacuate people to shelters |
| **1090** | **Free phone (IVR) number** to hear disaster early-warning messages |
| **999** | National emergency service (fire, police, ambulance) |
| **Fire Service and Civil Defence** | Rescue in fires, building collapses, floods |

- **Cyclone shelters (ঘূর্ণিঝড় আশ্রয়কেন্দ্র):** usually **multipurpose** — used as schools in normal times. **Killa (কিল্লা):** raised earthen mounds to protect **livestock**.
- Bangladesh's cyclone deaths have fallen sharply (about 3–5 lakh in 1970 → about 1.4 lakh in 1991 → a few thousand in Sidr 2007 → very few in recent cyclones), which is widely cited as a **global model of community-based preparedness**.

## International frameworks 🔥
| Framework | Year / place | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Yokohama Strategy** | 1994, Yokohama, Japan | First global DRR strategy |
| **Hyogo Framework for Action** | **2005–2015**, adopted in **Kobe (Hyogo), Japan** | Building resilience of nations and communities |
| 🔥 **Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction** | **2015–2030**, adopted in **Sendai, Japan (March 2015)** | **4 priorities** and **7 global targets** — reduce disaster deaths, affected people, economic losses and damage to infrastructure; more early warning |

- **UNDRR** (UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction) leads global DRR work.
- **13 October:** International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction.
- **10 March:** National Disaster Preparedness Day in Bangladesh.

## Key terms
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Vulnerability (ঝুঁকিপূর্ণতা/অরক্ষিততা)** | How easily people or assets can be harmed |
| **Resilience (সহনশীলতা)** | Ability to resist, absorb and recover from a disaster |
| **Capacity** | Strengths and resources available to cope |
| **DRR** | Disaster Risk Reduction |
| **CBDRM** | Community-Based Disaster Risk Management |
| **Contingency plan** | Advance plan for a specific expected emergency |
| **Evacuation** | Moving people from danger to safe places |

## Quick revision
- Cycle: **Mitigation → Preparedness → Response → Recovery**.
- Early warning and drills = **preparedness**; embankments/building codes = **mitigation**; rescue = **response**; rehabilitation = **recovery**.
- SOD: **1997, 2010, 2019** (latest).
- Disaster Management Act: **2012**; policy: **2015**.
- NDMC headed by the **Prime Minister/Head of Government**; DDMC by the **DC**; UDMC by the **UP Chairman**.
- Cyclone warnings: **BMD**; flood warnings: **FFWC (BWDB)**.
- CPP: **1972**, Government + **Bangladesh Red Crescent**.
- Sendai Framework: **2015–2030**, 7 targets; Hyogo: 2005–2015.

> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the year and place of each convention and what it deals with — Ramsar (wetlands, Iran, 1971), CBD (biodiversity, Rio, 1992), Montreal (ozone, 1987), CITES, Basel, Stockholm and so on. A single table answers most questions.

## Master table of conventions 🔥🔥
| Convention | Signed / adopted (place, year) | Deals with | Key extra fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Ramsar Convention** | **Ramsar, Iran, 2 February 1971** (in force 1975) | **Wetlands of international importance** | **2 February = World Wetlands Day**; oldest modern global environmental treaty |
| **World Heritage Convention** | **Paris (UNESCO), 1972** | Cultural and natural heritage | Sundarbans listed 1997 |
| 🔥 **CITES** | **Washington DC, 3 March 1973** (in force 1975) | **International trade in endangered species** of wild animals and plants | **3 March = World Wildlife Day**; secretariat Geneva |
| **CMS (Bonn Convention)** | **Bonn, Germany, 1979** | **Migratory species** of wild animals | |
| **UNCLOS** | **Montego Bay, Jamaica, 1982** | Law of the sea | EEZ 200 nautical miles |
| **Vienna Convention** | **Vienna, 1985** | Framework for **protecting the ozone layer** | |
| 🔥 **Montreal Protocol** | **Montreal, Canada, 16 September 1987** (in force 1989) | **Phasing out ozone-depleting substances (CFCs, halons)** | **16 September = Ozone Day**; universally ratified; **Kigali Amendment (2016)** phases down **HFCs** |
| 🔥 **Basel Convention** | **Basel, Switzerland, 1989** (in force 1992) | **Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes** | Stops rich countries dumping waste in poor ones |
| 🔥 **UNFCCC** | **Rio de Janeiro, 1992** (in force 1994) | **Climate change** | Yearly **COP**; secretariat Bonn |
| 🔥 **CBD (Convention on Biological Diversity)** | **Rio de Janeiro, 1992** (in force **29 December 1993**) | **Biodiversity** | Secretariat **Montreal**; **22 May = International Day for Biological Diversity** |
| **UNCCD** (Desertification) | **Paris, 1994** (in force 1996) | **Desertification and land degradation** | **17 June = Desertification and Drought Day** |
| **Kyoto Protocol** | **Kyoto, Japan, 1997** (in force 2005) | Binding greenhouse-gas cuts for developed countries | Under UNFCCC |
| **Rotterdam Convention** | **Rotterdam, 1998** | **Prior informed consent** for trade in hazardous **chemicals and pesticides** | |
| **Cartagena Protocol** | **2000** | **Biosafety** — safe handling of **living modified organisms (GMOs)** | Under CBD |
| 🔥 **Stockholm Convention** | **Stockholm, 2001** (in force 2004) | **Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)**, e.g. DDT, dioxins | Not to be confused with the 1972 Stockholm Conference |
| **Nagoya Protocol** | **Nagoya, Japan, 2010** | **Access and benefit-sharing** from genetic resources | Under CBD |
| **Minamata Convention** | **Kumamoto, Japan, 2013** (in force 2017) | **Mercury** | Named after Minamata disease (mercury poisoning) |
| 🔥 **Paris Agreement** | **Paris, December 2015** (in force 2016) | Climate: well below 2 °C, aim 1.5 °C | Under UNFCCC |
| **Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework** | **Montreal, December 2022 (CBD COP15)** | New biodiversity targets to 2030 | **"30 by 30"**: protect **30% of land and 30% of oceans by 2030** |

**Memory hooks**
- **"Ramsar = Wetland, Iran, '71"**; **"Montreal = Ozone, '87"**; **"Basel = Waste, '89"**; **"Stockholm 2001 = POPs"**; **"Rotterdam = chemicals (PIC)"**; **"Minamata = Mercury"**.
- **Rio 1992 gave three "Rio conventions":** **UNFCCC, CBD** (signed there) and **UNCCD** (negotiated as a result, adopted 1994).

## CBD in detail 🔥
- Opened for signature at the **Earth Summit, Rio, 5 June 1992**.
- 🔥 **Three objectives:**
  1. **Conservation** of biological diversity
  2. **Sustainable use** of its components
  3. **Fair and equitable sharing of benefits** from genetic resources
- **Protocols:** **Cartagena (biosafety, 2000)** and **Nagoya (access and benefit-sharing, 2010)**.
- The **USA** has signed but **not ratified** the CBD.

## Ramsar Convention in detail 🔥
- Full name: **Convention on Wetlands of International Importance, especially as Waterfowl Habitat**.
- Signed at **Ramsar, Iran**, on **2 February 1971**.
- **Montreux Record:** list of Ramsar sites whose ecology is under threat.
- 🔥 **Bangladesh** joined in **1992**. **Ramsar sites of Bangladesh:** **Sundarbans (1992)** and **Tanguar Haor (2000)**.

## Major environment conferences 🔥
| Conference | Year / place | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **UN Conference on the Human Environment** | **Stockholm, June 1972** | **First global environment conference**; created **UNEP** (HQ **Nairobi**, Kenya); led to **World Environment Day (5 June)** |
| **Brundtland Commission report *Our Common Future*** | **1987** | Defined **sustainable development**: meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs |
| 🔥 **Earth Summit (UNCED)** | **Rio de Janeiro, June 1992** | **Agenda 21**, Rio Declaration, UNFCCC, CBD, Forest Principles |
| **World Summit on Sustainable Development (Rio+10)** | **Johannesburg, 2002** | |
| **Rio+20** | **Rio, 2012** | *The Future We Want*; started the process leading to the **SDGs (2015)** |

## Bangladesh's own environmental laws (quick list)
- **Department of Environment (DoE)** set up in **1989**.
- **Environment Policy 1992** (updated **2018**).
- 🔥 **Environment Conservation Act 1995** — basis for **Ecologically Critical Areas (ECA)** and environmental clearance.
- **Wildlife (Conservation and Security) Act 2012**; **Biodiversity Act 2017**.

## Quick revision
- Ramsar: **wetlands, Iran, 1971**; World Wetlands Day **2 February**.
- CITES: **trade in endangered species, Washington, 1973**.
- Montreal Protocol: **ozone, 1987**; Kigali Amendment **2016** (HFCs).

- CBD: **Rio 1992**, in force **1993**, three objectives; Cartagena (biosafety), Nagoya (ABS).
- Stockholm Conference **1972** → **UNEP (Nairobi)** and World Environment Day.
- Kunming–Montreal Framework (2022): **30 by 30**.
- Bangladesh Ramsar sites: **Sundarbans, Tanguar Haor**.

GEO-11.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask Malthus's theory, demographic terms (TFR, density, sex ratio, dependency ratio), world and Bangladesh population facts from the 2022 census, megacities, and push–pull migration theory. Figures change, so learn the year with each number.

## Key demographic terms 🔥
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Demography (জনমিতি)** | Scientific study of population |
| **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** | Live births per **1,000** people per year |
| **Crude Death Rate (CDR)** | Deaths per **1,000** people per year |
| **Natural growth rate** | CBR − CDR (migration not counted) |
| 🔥 **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** | Average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. **Replacement level ≈ 2.1** |
| **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)** | Deaths of babies under **1 year** per **1,000 live births** |
| **Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)** | Maternal deaths per **1,00,000 live births** |
| 🔥 **Population density** | People per **square kilometre** |
| 🔥 **Sex ratio** | Number of **males per 100 females** (in Bangladesh) |
| **Dependency ratio** | Dependants (0–14 and 65+) per 100 working-age people (15–64) |
| 🔥 **Demographic dividend** | Economic boost when the **working-age share** of the population is large — Bangladesh is in this phase now |
| **Census (আদমশুমারি / জনশুমারি)** | Official count of the whole population, usually every 10 years |

## Population theories 🔥
- 🔥 **Thomas Robert Malthus**, *An Essay on the Principle of Population* (**1798**): population grows in a **geometric progression** (1, 2, 4, 8…) but food supply only in an **arithmetic progression** (1, 2, 3, 4…). **Positive checks** (famine, disease, war) and **preventive checks** (late marriage, moral restraint) control population.
- **Demographic Transition Model:** societies move from **high birth and death rates** → falling death rates (population explodes) → falling birth rates → **low birth and death rates** (stable). Linked with **Warren Thompson** and **Frank Notestein**.
- **Optimum population:** the size giving the highest income per person.
- **Population pyramid:** broad base = young, fast-growing (expansive); narrow base = ageing (constrictive).

## World population 🔥
- World population reached **8 billion on 15 November 2022** (UN). It was about **8.2 billion in 2025**.
- 🔥 **India** became the **most populous country in 2023**, passing **China** (UN estimate).
- **11 July = World Population Day** (started by UNDP in 1989, after the "Day of Five Billion", 11 July 1987).
- **UNFPA** (UN Population Fund): started **1969**, HQ **New York**.
- Most densely populated country (excluding city-states such as Monaco and Singapore): **Bangladesh** is among the highest in the world.

## Bangladesh population (Census 2022) 🔥🔥
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Census | **Population and Housing Census 2022** — the **6th** census after independence and the **first digital census**; held **15–21 June 2022** by **BBS** |
| Previous censuses | **1974**, 1981, 1991, 2001, **2011** |

| Adjusted population (after the post-enumeration check) | **About 16.98 crore** |

| 🔥 Sex ratio | **About 98** (98.07 males per 100 females) — **women outnumber men** |
| Annual growth rate (2011–2022) | **About 1.22%** |
| Urban population | **About 31.5%** |
| Literacy (age 7+) | **About 75%** |
| Most populous division / district | **Dhaka** / **Dhaka** |
| Least populous district | **Bandarban** |

- Bangladesh's **TFR** is now about **2.0–2.2** (close to replacement level) and life expectancy about **72 years** (BBS Sample Vital Statistics, 2023).

> 🔄 Update: check the latest Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics and Bangladesh Economic Review for current TFR, life expectancy and growth rate.

## Urbanization (নগরায়ণ) 🔥
- **Urbanization:** the growing share of people living in **towns and cities**.
- **Causes (push–pull):** rural poverty, river erosion, landlessness, disasters (**push**); jobs (garment industry), education, health care, services in cities (**pull**).
- More than **half the world's people** now live in urban areas (the UN estimated **55% in 2018**, rising towards **68% by 2050**).
- 🔥 **Megacity:** a city with **10 million or more** people. **Dhaka** is one of the world's largest and most densely populated megacities.
  - The UN's older ranking (World Urbanization Prospects 2018) put **Tokyo** first. Its **2025** revision, using a new definition of cities, ranked **Jakarta** first and **Dhaka** second, and projects Dhaka to become the largest by about 2050.
- **Primate city:** a city far larger than any other in the country (idea by **Mark Jefferson**, 1939). **Dhaka** is the primate city of Bangladesh.
- **Conurbation:** several cities that grow together into one urban area. **Urban sprawl:** unplanned spread of a city outward. **Counter-urbanization:** people moving out of cities to rural areas.
- **Problems:** slums, traffic congestion, waterlogging, air pollution, housing and water shortages.

> 🔄 Update: city rankings change with each UN revision; check the latest.

## Migration (অভিবাসন) 🔥
- **Migration:** movement of people from one place to another to live.
- **Internal** (within a country, e.g. rural → urban) vs **international** (across borders). **Emigration** = leaving a country; **immigration** = entering a country.
- 🔥 **Laws of migration:** **E. G. Ravenstein** (1885). **Push–pull theory:** **Everett Lee** (1966).
- **Brain drain:** skilled and educated people leaving the country.
- **Remittance:** money sent home by migrants — a major source of foreign exchange for Bangladesh.
- **Climate migrants:** people forced to move by sea-level rise, erosion, cyclones and salinity.
- **Refugee:** a person who flees their country because of persecution or war. **Rohingya:** over **one million** live in camps in **Cox's Bazar**, most arriving after **August 2017**; some have been relocated to **Bhasan Char** (Noakhali).
- **Institutions:** **BMET** (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training, 1976) handles overseas employment; **IOM** (International Organization for Migration, 1951, HQ **Geneva**); **UNHCR** (UN Refugee Agency, 1950, **Geneva**).
- **18 December = International Migrants Day**.

## Quick revision
- Malthus (**1798**): population **geometric**, food **arithmetic**.
- Replacement-level TFR ≈ **2.1**.
- World population **8 billion on 15 November 2022**; most populous country: **India (2023)**.
- World Population Day: **11 July**.
- Bangladesh Census 2022: **16.51 crore** enumerated; density **~1,119/sq km**; sex ratio **~98**; growth **1.22%**; urban **~31.5%**.
- Megacity = **10 million+**; Dhaka is Bangladesh's **primate city**.
- Laws of migration: **Ravenstein**; push–pull: **Everett Lee**.
- International Migrants Day: **18 December**.

> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the three types of rock with examples (granite, sandstone, marble), metamorphic changes (limestone → marble), Earth's layers, Wegener's continental drift, plate boundary types, how the Himalayas formed, and famous volcanoes and the "Ring of Fire".

## Earth's interior 🔥
| Layer | Depth / facts |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Crust (ভূত্বক)** | Thinnest layer. **Continental crust** about **30–70 km** (lighter, granite-type, **SIAL** = silica + aluminium); **oceanic crust** about **5–10 km** (heavier, basalt-type, **SIMA** = silica + magnesium) |
| **Mantle (গুরুমণ্ডল)** | Down to about **2,900 km**; hot, partly molten upper part (**asthenosphere**) on which the plates move |
| 🔥 **Core (কেন্দ্রমণ্ডল)** | **Outer core liquid**, **inner core solid**; made mostly of **nickel and iron (NIFE)**; Earth's magnetic field comes from the moving outer core |

- **Lithosphere** = crust + uppermost solid mantle (broken into plates).
- **Boundaries (discontinuities):** **Mohorovičić (Moho)** — crust/mantle; **Gutenberg** — mantle/core; **Lehmann** — outer/inner core.
- 🔥 **Most abundant elements in the crust:** **oxygen (about 46%)**, **silicon (about 28%)**, **aluminium (most abundant metal)**, iron.

## Rocks (শিলা) 🔥🔥
| Type | How formed | Features | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Igneous (আগ্নেয় শিলা)** | Cooling and hardening of **magma/lava** | Called the **primary rock**; no layers, no fossils; crystalline | **Intrusive/plutonic** (cooled slowly underground, large crystals): **granite**, gabbro. **Extrusive/volcanic** (cooled quickly on surface): **basalt**, pumice, obsidian |
| 🔥 **Sedimentary (পাললিক শিলা)** | Layers of **sediment** (sand, mud, shells) pressed and cemented over time | **Layered (strata)**; **contain fossils**; cover about **75% of the land surface** (but a small share of the crust's volume); hold **coal, oil and gas** | **Sandstone, limestone, shale, conglomerate, coal**, chalk |
| 🔥 **Metamorphic (রূপান্তরিত শিলা)** | Existing rocks changed by great **heat and pressure** | Harder, often banded/foliated | **Marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist** |

### Metamorphic changes 🔥
| Original rock | Becomes |
|---|---|
| **Limestone** | **Marble** |
| **Sandstone** | **Quartzite** |
| **Shale / clay** | **Slate** |
| **Granite** | **Gneiss** |
| **Coal** | **Graphite** (via anthracite) |

- **Rock cycle:** igneous → weathering → sediments → sedimentary → heat/pressure → metamorphic → melting → magma → igneous again.
- **Bangladesh:** most of the land is made of **loose sedimentary deposits (alluvium)**. **Hard rock (granite-type)** is mined at **Maddhapara, Dinajpur**; **coal** at **Barapukuria, Dinajpur**; **limestone** in Sunamganj and **Joypurhat**.

## Continental drift and plate tectonics 🔥🔥
- 🔥 **Alfred Wegener** (German) proposed **continental drift** (**1912**; book *The Origin of Continents and Oceans*, 1915).
- About 250–300 million years ago all continents formed one supercontinent, 🔥 **Pangaea**, surrounded by the ocean **Panthalassa**. Pangaea split into **Laurasia** (north) and **Gondwanaland** (south), separated by the **Tethys Sea**.
- Evidence: fit of coastlines (South America–Africa), matching fossils and rocks across oceans.
- **Sea-floor spreading** (**Harry Hess**, 1960s) and **plate tectonics theory** (1960s) explained how continents move.
- **Plates:** large, rigid pieces of the lithosphere moving a few cm a year. **Major plates:** **Pacific (largest)**, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian (often split into Indian and Australian), Antarctic.

### Plate boundaries 🔥
| Boundary | Movement | Result | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔥 **Divergent (constructive)** | Plates **move apart** | New crust forms; **mid-ocean ridges**, rift valleys | **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, Iceland, **East African Rift Valley** |
| 🔥 **Convergent (destructive)** | Plates **move towards each other** | **Subduction**, ocean trenches, volcanoes, **fold mountains**, earthquakes | **Himalayas** (Indian plate hitting Eurasian plate), **Andes**, **Mariana Trench**, Japan |
| **Transform (conservative)** | Plates **slide past** each other | Earthquakes; crust neither made nor destroyed | **San Andreas Fault**, California |

- 🔥 The **Himalayas** are **young fold mountains** formed by the collision of the **Indian and Eurasian plates**; they are still rising slowly.

### Types of mountains
| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Fold mountains** (most common, highest) | **Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies**, Atlas |
| **Block mountains** (from faulting: horst and graben) | Vosges (France), Black Forest (Germany), Sierra Nevada |
| **Volcanic mountains** | **Mount Fuji** (Japan), **Kilimanjaro**, Mauna Loa |
| **Residual mountains** (worn-down old mountains) | **Aravalli** (India), Eastern Ghats |

## Volcanoes (আগ্নেয়গিরি) 🔥
- A **volcano** is an opening in the crust through which **magma, gases and ash** erupt.
- **Magma** = molten rock **below** the surface; **lava** = molten rock **on** the surface.
- Parts: **magma chamber**, **vent**, **crater** (opening at the top). **Caldera:** a very large crater formed when the top collapses.
- **By activity:** **active** (erupts now or recently: **Etna**, **Stromboli**, **Kilauea**, **Mauna Loa**), **dormant** (sleeping, may erupt again), **extinct** (not expected to erupt again).
- **By shape:** **shield volcano** (broad, gentle slopes, runny lava — **Mauna Loa**), **composite/stratovolcano** (steep cone, explosive — **Fuji, Vesuvius**), cinder cone.

| Famous volcano / event | Fact |
|---|---|
| 🔥 **Vesuvius** (Italy) | Buried **Pompeii** and Herculaneum in **79 CE** |
| **Stromboli** (Italy) | Called the **"Lighthouse of the Mediterranean"** |
| **Etna** (Sicily, Italy) | Europe's highest active volcano |
| **Mauna Loa** (Hawaii) | **Largest active volcano** on Earth |
| **Krakatoa** (Indonesia) | Huge eruption in **1883** |
| **Tambora** (Indonesia) | **1815**, largest eruption in recorded history → 1816 **"Year Without a Summer"** |
| **Mount St. Helens** (USA) | Major eruption in 1980 |
| **Ojos del Salado** (Chile–Argentina) | Highest active volcano |

- 🔥 **Pacific "Ring of Fire":** a horseshoe-shaped belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean; about **75% of the world's active volcanoes** are here.
- **Indonesia** has the most active volcanoes of any country. **Iceland** is called the **"Land of Fire and Ice"**.
- **Hot spot:** a fixed plume of magma under a plate (**Hawaii**).
- **Geyser:** hot spring that shoots water and steam (**Old Faithful**, Yellowstone, USA); the word comes from **Geysir** in Iceland.
- Bangladesh has **no active volcano**.

## Quick revision
- Earth: **crust → mantle → core** (core = **NIFE**, outer core liquid).
- Crust's most abundant element: **oxygen**; metal: **aluminium**.
- Igneous = **primary rock** (granite, basalt); sedimentary = **layers and fossils**; metamorphic = heat/pressure.
- **Limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; shale → slate; granite → gneiss.**
- Continental drift: **Alfred Wegener**; supercontinent **Pangaea**.
- Himalayas: **Indian + Eurasian plate collision** (convergent, fold mountains).
- Mid-Atlantic Ridge = **divergent**; San Andreas = **transform**.
- Vesuvius buried **Pompeii (79 CE)**; Stromboli = **Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**; Ring of Fire = **Pacific**.
